summary: Import AI 第482期围绕三大主题展开：华为内核基准测试、空中无人机检测以及一座国家实验室的AI科学基准。本期随笔部分探讨'科学方法是否可能是涌现的'这一问题。
context: 该周刊一期覆盖硬件基准、安全探测与AI科研评测等多个方向，适合快速浏览行业多领域动态。
contentHtml:
Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers.

Subscribe now

Chinese researchers optimize Huawei chips with a kernel improvement benchmark:
…AscendGYM will help China do its own form of RSI…
Researchers with the Shenzhen Loop Area Institute, a Chinese research organization, have built and released AscendGYM, “a kernel optimization benchmark for Ascend NPUs”. The purpose of AscendGYM is to make it easier to use AI to develop custom kernels for Ascend chips from Huawei - especially important given the export controls that prevent Chinese organizations from acquiring frontier Western semiconductors and forcing them onto Huawei.

What AscendGYM does and contains: The goal is for AscendGYM to be the best way to evaluate the efficacy of AI-designed kernels as well as design new ones. The software is meant to help researchers answer this question: “Given a correct kernel implementation, can the specific agent further improve its performance for a target workload within an acceptable budget while preserving correctness?,” they write.
“AscendGYM evaluates performance across multiple deployment cases, the best achievable performance for specific shapes and scenarios, and the optimization cost required to obtain these gains. Together, these dimensions characterize cross-case applicability, shape specialization, and optimization efficiency.”
The software includes the AscendForge evaluation environment, which provides unified interfaces for “compilation, correctness checking, performance measurement, and feedback”.

How well can AI models optimize Ascend chips? In tests, the single best model is Opus 5, followed by GPT-5.6, followed by GLM-5.3. They test out models in Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode; Claude Code yields the best absolute scores, and GLM does well in it, while GPT does well in Codex. Opus 5 is more token hungry and GPT-5.6 more token efficient.

Why this matters - ingredients for Chinese RSI: For AI systems to be able to build themselves, they need to be able to develop and improve the software that is used for their own training and inference. Software like AscendGYM will be an essential ingredient for allowing China to rapidly improve the efficiency of its own compute substrates. The software will also have a bearing on export controls, where it provides a route to improve the performance of Chinese chips and close the gap with Western alternatives.
Read more: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs (arXiv).
Get AscendGYM here: AscendGYM (GitHub).

***

Lawrence Livermore scientists test out if AI scientists can communicate uncertainty about experimental results:
…Can AI systems be appropriately conservative?...
“An agent that reports a confident wrong number is worse than one that reports honest uncertainty, because nobody downstream can tell the difference,” write researchers from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in a new paper that tests out how reliably AI systems can give accurate score ranges even when dealing with uncertainty.

Testing for uncertainty: The paper introduces SciResearch-Eval, “an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material’s thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator”. The novel part of this eval is that “an agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth”.

What they studied: They give AI agents a common materials science task - measuring a material’s thermal properties by heating a sample and fitting a heat-conduction model to its temperature response.
“An agent receives a sample of unknown material, a simulator of heat conduction through it, one heating experiment, and budgets: four more experiments it designs, compute for simulations and fits, and a cap on actions. It must report the sample’s conductivity, heat capacity and rear heat-transfer coefficient with 95% intervals, and predict a measurement it may not run,” they write. “Hidden from the agent, the simulator may be under-resolved, physically wrong (the real sample has temperature-dependent conductivity, a glued joint, front-face radiation, or heat loss through its sides), or adequate but fed uninformative data”.

Results - only the most powerful frontier models can do this: “When the simulator is missing real physics, only GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2 are reliable at default settings; the Claude 5.5 models recover only at their highest reasoning setting, and older and open-weight models not at all.”
These models are able to do well by automatically trying to measure where the simulator is accurate and where it is less accurate then bases their estimates on that, making them more resilient to the different ways the simulator gets broken in experiments.

Why this matters - real scientists are careful, and so are powerful models: Papers like this are further indications that we’re entering an era of AI-driven science. Though many of today’s models can assist in scientific experiments, as this paper shows only a couple of the powerful models at the frontier are able to operate with such appropriate autonomous skepticism and inherent attendance to the scientific method that they can deal with unanticipated breaks in their equipment. This is both an indication of the science advancement to come and a sign of how the most powerful models are exhibiting more and more of an ability to generalize and make themselves robust to perturbations in their environment.
Read more: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents (arXiv).
Check out the leaderboard here (official site).

***

Stanford professors launch AI startup that wants to create a world where thousands of models define the frontier:
…Noeri sees two well-regarded AI researchers enter the neolab game…
Stanford profs Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin have launched Noeri, “a neolab to push the frontier of plural intelligence”. They have raised $110m and are relatively light on technical details, but their main vision is that they want to create a world where the frontier is defined by powerful models which rely on the proprietary data of distinct organizations. “Rather than one monolithic source of truth, we can nurture many small, specialized intelligences, each tuned to a place, a people or a problem,” they write.

Further details: “At Noeri, we are building intelligence that learns proactively and continually. Most AI today is trained once and then frozen, while the world it serves keeps moving,” they write. “We close that gap with living systems that grow out of our own research. Our work on test-time training showed that learning on the job after deployment can unlock new capabilities and lead to new discoveries. Our work on self-distillation found that a model can become its own teacher, learning from each mistake and solving hard problems in far fewer attempts. And our work on agentic orchestration demonstrated that a small model conducting a team of other models and tools can outperform frontier models at a fraction of the cost.”

Why this matters - the political economy of the singularity: Currently, the dominant AI models are massive pre-trained ones from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI and a tiny handful of other companies. What would it mean for the frontier to be instead defined by a broader set of actors? This is a core question inherent to the political economy of AI and startups like this show how some people are going to try and utilize technical approaches to make that different vision a reality.
Read more in the announcement tweet from Yejin (Yejin Choi, X).
Check out the official site here (Noeri).

***

Chinese researchers build an air-to-air drone identification set:
…A2A-UAV will help people add more visual intelligence to drones…
Researchers with Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology have developed and released A2A-UAV, “a multimodal dataset for air-to-air UAV detection and identification”. This kind of dataset has obvious civil and military applications and will be used to create better AI systems for autonomous onboard sensing on drones.

What A2A-UAV consists of: 105,263 samples, split roughly equally across three different locations - a playground, a park, and a garden - and also split equally across day and night. “Each sample provides one RGB image and one panoramic image for annotation”, as well as thermal images, RF time-frequency images, a radar point cloud, and metadata. Bounding boxes are provided for the RGB and panoramic images, but not the other ones.
One use case of this dataset could be to try and extend annotations to the other modalities: “Specifically, the bounding boxes can be transferred to the thermal images to support thermal UAV detection, and the radar points can be associated with the visual targets to support radar-based UAV localization,” the researchers write.
The full dataset comprises 271 independently extractable .tar.gz archives with a total size of approximately 2.5 TB.

How the data was collected: “The data were acquired by a UAV-mounted platform equipped with an RGB-thermal gimbal camera, a panoramic camera, an RF spectrum analyzer, and a millimeter-wave radar,” they write. The data includes 15 target drones from 13 commercial models, including three separately labeled DJI Mini 4 Pro units.

Why this matters - fuel for the physical world: Datasets like this are the ingredients for making it easier for AI systems to operate robots and drones in the physical world. They also have potential dual use impacts, though my suspicion is that datasets like this are pretty irrelevant to militaries relative to the kinds of datasets that - and I’m speculating wildly here - might be being gathered in Ukraine right now given the extremely sophisticated drone-to-drone conflict there.
Read more: A2A-UAV: A Multimodal Air-to-Air Dataset for UAV Detection and Identification (arXiv).
Get a sample of the data from Google Drive here (Google Drive).
The full dataset will ultimately be available via Baidu Netdisk with the extraction code A2AD (direct link, Baidu Netdisk).

***

Tech Tales:

Machine architecture and the objectivity crisis of Machine Hermeneutics
[Memoir from a primary Machine Hermeneutics investigator, 2033]

“We shape our buildings; thereafter they shape us” - Winston Churchill, human politician, 1943.

The building was a vast representation of the proposed Upgrade Device and we walked around it, our footsteps echoing as the sound bounced off its curving walls, eventually dimming in the face of the baroque crenellations that covered the edges of every surface. We humans, a small group of us, the best of our kind, needed to make sense of this building and explain the science it represented, and only then could it be used.

As per the terms of the Sentience Accords, any novel machine-designed insight or equipment needed to be fully explainable by humans before the machines would be allowed to use it. In the early years, this so-called “conceptual verification” had mostly been a matter of time: machines performed science and delivered new insights to the world, then humans studied these insights and made sense of them, eventually generating human-readable explanations of the machine logic. Once this was complete, whatever insights or tools that had been created could be used.

But as the machines grew more advanced and their science went further, the work became more arduous: machines would invent ideas, then use these ideas to inform the design of new experimental equipment, and then use this equipment as the basis of some new discovery. To keep up, the humans had to understand each link in the chain as well as the chain itself.

This flood of scientific progress had caused the field of machine hermeneutics to come into existence in the mid-2020s. By the 2030s, the pinnacle of human achievement in the sciences was considered to be neither making breakthroughs nor wielding AI systems to advance science, but rather to be able to generate elegant, pedagogically useful explanations of the frontiers of machine science, so that other humans could build a mental map of this new territory.

Thus had come into being the new field of didactic architecture; vast buildings meant to give experts in machine hermeneutics a better conceptual understanding of what the machines had built. These buildings were constructed through the interplay of humans and machines. The first had been crude, little more than 3D printed extrusions inside otherwise normal houses or apartments. But exposure to the buildings had verifiably sped up human understanding, with clear TTHUE (Time-to-human-understandable-explanation) improvements visible in cohorts of machine hermeneutics experts that experienced the buildings and those that didn’t. This led to its own arms race, with some of us specializing in the construction of the buildings as our primary work. We raced with one another, building ever more complicated spaces that could impart knowledge of ever more alien concepts.

We had all been electrons, appearing and disappearing in 3D transistors. We had been qubits, placed into spheres that rolled around vomit-inducingly when our position was indeterminate, then resolving us up or down at the moment of delivering an answer. We had laid our hands on surfaces suggestive of the textures and arrangements of novel forms of heat shield and solar panel.

Once I had walked for six miles through corridors meant to suggest the path a plasma might take through a fusion reactor, and instead of magnets I was buffeted on all sides by wind that forced me into the center of the paths.

The building meant to educate us about the Upgrade Device was larger than anything we’d seen before and was replete with ideas from many earlier machine inventions. All around us were indicators of complexity packed up into familiar architectural tropes that many of us had studied to understand past inventions. We dispersed throughout the building, walking its many levels and exploring its passages. At night we gathered in the entrance hall for a spartan dinner served at a low table, finding ourselves whispering to one another even though no one forced us to.

It had begun to feel to us as though the building was doing something more than teaching us - that in its various chambers there was something else being taught to us. Something about understanding the minds behind the concepts that it sought to explain to us. That in spending all of our effort on understanding the products of the machines perhaps we were being taught to think like them and behave as them.

Things that inspired this story: The singularity which has already begun; the rise of AI science; how when you look at things like the machine math papers that have proliferated this year you realize we may spend tens or hundreds of times more time on understanding them as people than the machines did in generating them; architecture; multi-modal representations.

Thanks for reading!

title: Cloudflare 如何探测 DNS
originalTitle: Probing DNS at Cloudflare
author: Doug Aaser
summary: Cloudflare 分享了其 DNS 探测的工程实践：公司构建了可扩展的内部测试框架，支持各团队为网络协议搭建专用测试工具。这套框架已被用于 DNS，文章讲述了从通用测试能力到 DNS 探测工具的落地过程。
context: 对需要为网络协议搭建自动化测试的工程团队，Cloudflare 内部测试框架的落地思路有直接参考价值。
contentHtml:
Imagine this: you’ve just pushed a release. All the unit tests passed and your dashboards are green. You sit back to relax but then suddenly your phone starts blowing up: prod is broken.

This is something the Cloudflare DNS team has experienced firsthand. In one rollout of the service that publishes DNS records to our edge, a scheduling bug let some record changes sit unpublished for hours. The service stayed up and was healthy, but new hostnames were slow to resolve and certificates couldn't be issued until the bug was squashed.

DNS failures are hard to catch because they are slow, spread across the network, and partial in where they cause impact. We needed to figure out a way to test DNS the way customers experience it: constantly, from every data center, and against production.

For us, the answer was to extend Flamingo, the end-to-end testing framework we were already using to run hundreds of millions of tests a day against Cloudflare's edge. This post covers how Flamingo's modular design lets us add DNS support, how we measure propagation, and how those measurements now decide whether a release goes ahead or gets rolled back.

A little background

At Cloudflare we’re obsessed with improving performance and safety for our customers. It’s crucial that our code is tested constantly, both at scale and against the real Cloudflare edge that our users operate in. That’s one reason why we created a tool called Flamingo: to measure the behavior of our production environments and make sure that code in lower-tier environments behaves as expected.

We’ve already written a little about how this tool has been used in the upgrades to our CDN stack. However, this is only a small portion of how we use Flamingo internally. One of the features of Flamingo is its modular architecture that enables teams to extend the capabilities of the tool to speak other networking protocols. In our case, we wanted to use these modular capabilities to test DNS.

What is Flamingo?

Testing is hard. Testing at scale, when you have a widely distributed system, is even harder. There are many complex pathways that requests take and multiple systems that each network request must traverse before making its way to the origin. Unit testing alone is not nearly enough for this. We need to run constant automated testing against real systems and measure the outcomes of those requests to make informed decisions on the health of a service.

Enter Flamingo. Originally built around complex multi-step HTTP testing, its capabilities and scope have increased substantially over the years. Flamingo is built from the ground up with Cloudflare’s infrastructure in mind. We built a control plane and scheduler that let teams target specific environments, data centers, or percentages of metals. We needed to integrate with custom reporting, metrics, and analytics tooling. Additionally, it needed to be a tool with predictable performance and run well on bare-metal servers in resource-constrained environments.

Being delightful

When we’re building internal tooling like this, we strive to create a delightful developer experience. Internal tooling should be as easy as possible to use, but also powerful enough to handle over 80% of all use cases. And in order for a new edge acceptance test framework to be successful, it needs to be built in such a way that it forces teams to follow common guidelines and build reusable scripts in an environment that is stable, scalable, and manages complexity.

One thing that is not delightful is debugging a test. If you allow a user to write tests in a traditional programming language, when their test fails they then both need to debug the upstream system being tested and the test itself. This is why we built Flamingo to use a custom domain-specific language (DSL) consisting of a simple setup-request-response format.

For example, let’s imagine that we want to make sure we are redirecting all unencrypted traffic to its encrypted counterpart.

TEST test-redirect
SET $hostname www.cloudflare.com

GET "http://$(hostname)/"

ASSERT STATUS IS 301
ASSERT HEADER Location IS "https://$(hostname)/"

Here we can see the power of the DSL. In five lines of code, we have a script that can run anywhere on Cloudflare’s edge and scale to thousands of requests per minute. We can take the data produced from the millions of data points generated from this and turn those into a graph defining how our service is actually performing in the real world.

Taking the setup-request-response test format from above and modifying it slightly allows us to use Flamingo for more than just HTTP testing. Instead of the middle step being a request, we can now look at it as an action. Now we’ve changed our system from something that makes HTTP requests into something that can perform any action for which we’d like to measure the outcome.

In Flamingo we call these modules and have put immense effort into making them as easy as possible for anyone to write. Flamingo is written in Rust, due to its consistent performance characteristics and strong type system. The type system in particular lends itself to this modularity, by allowing us to use strongly-typed enumerations for input and output in the Flamingo action runner:

pub enum Action {
  Query {
    method: String,
    url: Expression,
    parameters: Vec<http::QueryParameters>,
  },
  DnsQuery {
    query_name: Expression,
    query_type: Expression,
    parameters: Vec<dns::DnsQueryParameters>,
  },
}

pub enum ActionOutput {
  Http(http::FetchResponse),
  Dns(dns::QueryResponse),
}

pub type ActionHandlerFunction = Arc<
  dyn Fn(
      Action,
      Arc<Ctx>,
      InterpreterConfig,
    )
      -> BoxFuture<'static, Result<ActionOutput>>
    + Send
    + Sync
    + 'static,
>;

pub type ActionHandlerLUT = Arc<
  dyn Fn(&Action) -> ActionHandlerFunction
    + Send
    + Sync
    + 'static,
>;

What we’ve done here is decouple the logic for performing an action (in this case an HTTP request) into a dynamically dispatched function that we can then call independently of other actions. This leaves things like test scheduling and resource management as higher-level operations that someone implementing a module doesn’t need to worry about. All the author needs to focus on is the logic.

pub async fn query(
  action: Action,
  ctx: Arc<Ctx>,
  cfg: InterpreterConfig,
) -> Result<ActionOutput> {
  let Action::Query {
    method,
    url,
    parameters,
  } = action
  else {
    bail!("Invalid action for module-http::query: {action:?}");
  };
  ...
}

pub async fn execute_module<F>(
  ctx: Arc<Ctx>,
  cfg: &InterpreterConfig,
  handler_lut: F,
) -> Result<ActionOutput>
where
  F: (Fn(&Action) -> ActionHandlerFunction),
{
  let func = handler_lut(action);
  let action_out = (func)(action.clone(), ctx.clone(), cfg.clone()).await?;
  ...
}

Using Flamingo to probe DNS

The adage says that when issues arise, it's always DNS. Like many jokes, there is always a kernel of truth behind it. DNS is an incredibly important piece of the Internet, and since it relies on a complex network of interconnected sources of truth, it can become easy for a single misstep to cause a storm of failures.

DNS can be a particularly finicky system due to its hierarchical nature. When you change a DNS record for a Cloudflare zone, for example, said record needs to be propagated to the authoritative servers such that the updated record becomes widely available. To reduce latency, records are stored in physically closer caches. These records have a time to live (TTL) associated with them that tells the local DNS cache how long before it needs to refetch that record from the authoritative server. Any delays will impact time-sensitive operations like certificate issuance and traffic failover.

We’ve already mentioned that we built Flamingo for extensibility. One of the first and most impactful modules in use today was built specifically for this use case. Our team was able to add code that extended Flamingo such that instead of sending HTTP requests, we send DNS queries. By doing so we got everything else for free. No need for the DNS team to worry about managing a new probing service. No need for them to have to integrate with our reporting pipelines. It all just worked.

To probe DNS, we measure how quickly customer record changes propagate to authoritative nameservers and the public resolver (1.1.1.1). The test continuously updates a TXT record with a timestamp and queries three authoritative nameserver IPs and 1.1.1.1 from every data center, asserting freshness within 90s (authoritative) and 600s (resolver).

TEST test-propagation-delay-direct-108-162-193-62
MOD dns

SET $hostname "some.probe.domain"
SET $authNs 108.162.193.62:53 # amir.ns.cloudflare.com

QUERY $hostname TXT
TARGET $authNs

ASSERT DNS.RCODE IS NOERROR
ASSERT DNS.FLAGS CONTAINS AA
ASSERT DNS.ANSWERS[0] GT SUBTRACT(TIMESTAMP(), "90")

Catching bugs (SLO and steady)

To ensure that our many systems are operating within expectations, we define what are called service-level objectives (SLOs) for observing things like availability or latency. SLOs are a percentage of some metric that is used as a target. Additionally, SLOs are measured through service-level indicators (SLIs) which are the actual series of measurements focused on the end-to-end experience that a user has when interacting with a system.

By constantly sending synthetic Flamingo traffic through our production systems, we can begin to then use that information to build a picture of what our actual end users are experiencing — and provide that data for our SLOs. When that synthetic traffic encounters issues then we can be pretty confident that Cloudflare customers are also hitting issues and triage accordingly.

Once we have this information, it allows us to make informed decisions when releasing a service. SLOs operate in terms of error budgets and burn rates. An error budget is the percentage of downtime that a service is willing to tolerate while the burn rate is the rate of change in that budget at any given time. This allows for an automated system to understand the severity of an issue. For example, burning 10% of your error budget over a three-day period might be some long running issue that, while not urgent, is affecting customers and needs to be dealt with. But if you were to burn 10% of your error budget within an hour, that means an incident is occurring and customer impact will be substantial if not fixed immediately.

Using these numbers, we can look at our SLOs while deploying and make informed decisions on the health of a service. Based on that information, we can tell our releasing systems to either promote a change or roll it back.

The road ahead

By moving DNS monitoring to Flamingo, we’ve created a system that can proactively detect DNS issues before they have the chance to spread to the rest of Cloudflare’s edge. If Flamingo detects a spike in propagation latency in a specific canary data center, we can automatically halt the rollout of a new software version before it impacts the rest of the Internet.

DNS is just the start for extending Flamingo. We currently have modules for testing TCP, UDP, WebSockets, and several more. Having a tool for quickly testing and monitoring services has enabled teams to deploy large changes safely without the need for a human to keep a constant watch.

If this kind of reliability engineering interests you, check out our careers page for open roles.

title: 美国情报机构跟踪英伟达丑闻人物与中国情报部门联系超一年
originalTitle: US spies tracked Nvidia scandal figure's ties to Chinese intelligence for over a year
author: Maximilian Schreiner
summary: 据《纽约时报》报道，美国情报机构对爱丽丝·黄与中国国家安全部的接触跟踪超过一年，监视期间她还与时任英伟达CEO黄仁勋保持秘密恋情。联邦调查人员正调查一个东南亚公司网络是否被用于向中国走私AI芯片、违反美国出口管制。黄仁勋定于12月1日在美国众议院作证。
context: 该案同时牵涉美国对华AI芯片出口管制执法与英伟达高层丑闻，国会作证或披露更多细节。
contentHtml:
The woman at the center of the Nvidia scandal was in contact with China's top spy agency for over a year, US intelligence reports show. Alice Huang communicated with China's Ministry of State Security from spring 2025 through this fall, according to the New York Times, citing US intelligence findings. The entire time, she was carrying on a secret affair with then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

US spy agencies had been tracking the contacts for more than a year. Alice Huang's business partner Kang Wei, whom she introduced to acquaintances as her husband, is also believed to have cooperated with the ministry. Federal investigators are now trying to determine whether the two used a web of companies across Southeast Asia to funnel Nvidia AI chips into China, skirting US export controls. Alice Huang's firm Megaspeed is part of that network.

Jensen Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month after the affair became public, along with reports of a second relationship. President Donald Trump tried to downplay the allegations and floated the idea of Huang returning to the company. Nvidia's board shut that down.

Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Nvidia to come clean about its chip sales to China before the company makes any decisions about its future leadership. Jensen Huang is set to testify behind closed doors before the US House of Representatives on December 1.
contentHtmlZh:
{"t": ["

美国情报报告显示，身处英伟达丑闻风暴中心的这名女子与中国最高间谍机构保持接触已超过一年。据《纽约时报》援引美国情报结论报道，Alice Huang 自 2025 年春季至今年秋季一直与中国国家安全部保持联络。在此期间，她与英伟达时任 CEO 黄仁勋一直保持着一段秘密恋情。

美国情报机构追踪这些接触已超过一年。Alice Huang 的商业伙伴 Kang Wei——她曾向熟人介绍为自己的丈夫——据信也曾与该部门合作。联邦调查人员目前正在试图确定两人是否利用横跨东南亚的公司网络将英伟达 AI 芯片输入中国，借此规避美国出口管制。Alice Huang 的公司 Megaspeed 正是该网络的一部分。

黄仁勋在本月早些时候这段恋情曝光后辞去了 CEO 职务，随后又有报道称他还有第二段感情关系。唐纳德·特朗普总统试图淡化这些指控，并提出了让黄仁勋回归公司的想法。英伟达董事会否决了这一提议。

与此同时，财政部长斯科特·贝森特要求英伟达如实说明其对华芯片销售情况，再对公司未来领导层作出任何决定。黄仁勋定于 12 月 1 日在美国众议院闭门作证。

"]}

title: 盘前：纳指期货涨3.68% 半导体等科技股领涨
summary: 周一盘前，美国纳指期货上涨3.68%，半导体等科技股领涨，股指期货正从此前人工智能相关股票的猛烈抛售中反弹。这轮抛售此前已导致标普500指数进入技术性回调区间。
source: 新浪财经 · 实时滚动
context: AI相关股票的抛售曾将标普500推入技术性回调区间，期指大幅反弹是市场能否企稳的重要信号。
contentHtml:
周一美国股指期货正从人工智能相关股票遭遇的猛烈抛售中反弹。此前，这轮抛售导致标普500指数进入技术性回调区间。与此同时，亚洲各地监管机构纷纷采取措施，以稳定金融市场。随着市场避险需求减弱，美国国债和日元承受下行压力。

　　截至发稿，道指期货涨2.17%，标普500指数期货涨3.04%，有望结束此前连续七个交易日的下跌。纳指期货涨3.68%，其中半导体及其他科技股领涨。

　　欧洲股市涨幅相对温和，斯托克600指数上涨0.8%。

　　上周，纳斯达克综合指数累计下跌10%，创下2020年3月新冠疫情引发市场暴跌以来最大单周跌幅。与此同时，市场波动加剧，华尔街所谓的“恐慌指数”VIX自2025年4月以来首次突破40。

　　上周，以芯片制造商为主要成分的台湾地区股市基准指数创下1990年以来最大单周跌幅。周一，台湾地区股市上涨2.1%，监管机构的支持措施帮助市场逐渐企稳。韩国KOSPI指数的抛售行情则进一步加剧，不过该指数从10个月低点反弹，跌幅收窄至约3.3%。

　　今年上半年，韩国KOSPI指数曾是全球表现最强劲的主要股票指数之一。由于投资者押注半导体需求激增，该指数在六个月内上涨超过一倍。然而，随着近期抛售潮持续，KOSPI指数已经较此前高点下跌约50%。韩国财政部长周一重申，如有必要，政府将采取措施稳定金融市场。

　　技术性反弹不可避免

　　经历了一段极其艰难的行情后，股市在新一周开局表现强劲。此前，美国民主党在中期选举中横扫国会，以及黄仁勋被迫离开英伟达，加剧了投资者对人工智能投资热潮的担忧。接下来，市场仍将接连迎来重要风险事件。本周即将公布美国通胀数据，而投资者也开始质疑，在当前环境下，美联储是否应该在下个月继续加息。

　　AlphaValue分析师Pierre-Yves Gauthier表示：“考虑到上周市场跌势如此猛烈，技术性反弹几乎不可避免，但我不认为这种反弹能够持续。”他认为，由于股票估值仍需要进一步下降，市场疲软态势可能持续一段时间。

　　德意志银行策略师Jim Reid表示，围绕AI交易的担忧已经蔓延至更广泛的金融市场，引发全球投资者降低风险敞口，并寻求流动性。他在报告中写道：“这已经不再只是一场科技股抛售。”

　　AI交易逻辑发生转变

　　自聊天机器人ChatGPT推出以来的约四年间，“AI交易”推动了广泛股票上涨，受益企业涵盖芯片制造商、网络交换机和电缆生产商，以及发电企业。投资者此前普遍押注，人工智能计算需求将出现爆炸式增长。

　　分析师指出，AI相关支出仍然保持强劲。摩根士丹利预计，明年超大规模云计算企业的资本支出将增长超过70%，突破1.6万亿美元。

　　然而，金融市场的情绪已经发生剧烈转变。

　　被称为“AI教父”的英伟达前首席执行官黄仁勋离职，引发投资者对这家芯片制造商商业战略的质疑，尤其是英伟达向部分客户提供融资支持的做法。

　　与此同时，人工智能行业领军企业Anthropic的上市表现不及预期，也显示交易员对AI股票的态度正在迅速变化。上周五，该公司在上市后的首个完整交易日收跌8.5%。

　　除了本周美国股市自身的表现外，市场接下来还将面临两项重要考验：计算机制造商戴尔将于周二公布的业绩及前景展望，以及美联储下个月是否会按照投资者预期进一步加息。

　　美国PCE驾到

　　在此之前，本周三即将公布的数据预计显示，美国10月经通胀调整后的个人消费支出较前一个月有所增长，表明尽管消费者对通胀感到担忧，但其消费意愿尚未受到明显抑制。与此同时，市场预计个人消费支出（PCE）物价指数同比上涨3.8%，与今年5月的涨幅持平，达到三年来最高水平。

　　XTB分析师Kathleen Brooks表示：“市场可能会非常庆幸感恩节假期即将到来，因为这能够为投资者提供一个急需的喘息机会。”她指出：“PCE数据，尤其是核心PCE，将非常重要，因为市场开始质疑，在股市持续下跌的情况下，美联储进一步加息是否明智。”

　　市场还没出现全面投降式抛售

　　高盛集团交易部门表示，上周的市场抛售已经创造了颇具吸引力的美股买入机会。不过，该行同时警告，投资者整体持仓水平仍然偏高，这意味着市场可能尚未出现推动持续性反弹所需的全面投降式抛售。

　　市场策略师指出，风险资产在新一周开局表现更加稳健，中期基本面前景仍然具有支撑作用。不过，当前市场波动性极高，随着美国感恩节假期临近，流动性将逐渐下降，而此前引发投资者担忧的根本问题并未消失。任何反弹都可能被多头投资者视为更好的退出机会，而不是一轮持续性复苏的开始。

　　华尔街知名策略师Ed Yardeni在大约两个月内第二次下调标普500指数年末目标点位。亚德尼研究公司总裁兼首席投资策略师Yardeni目前预计，标普500指数将在2026年底收于7500点，低于他今年9月已经下调至7900点的目标。

　　不过，这一最新预测仍意味着，标普500指数有望较上周五收盘水平反弹超过8%。Yardeni还表示，美国政府因有关英伟达及其他美国芯片制造商涉嫌通过间接渠道向海外市场销售芯片的指控而进一步收紧出口控制，相关消息也对半导体股票造成了严重冲击。

　　风险情绪依旧脆弱

　　周一，此前为投资者提供一定避险保护的资产普遍回落。美国国债价格下跌，短期国债领跌。美国10年期国债收益率上涨5个基点，至4.96%。作为欧元区债券市场基准的德国10年期国债收益率上涨2.2个基点，至3.32%。

　　日元兑美元走弱。美元兑一篮子货币从19个月高点回落。此前，上周股市遭遇猛烈抛售，促使交易员下调了对美联储下个月激进加息的预期。美元指数下跌0.2%，至103.6。

　　黄金则反弹2.3%，重新站上3600美元，日内涨幅超过80美元。布伦特原油价格跌破每桶92美元。

　　不过，铜价仍徘徊在今年3月以来的最低水平附近，表明市场风险偏好依然脆弱。

　　美股大跌之际，贝森特公开反对美联储继续紧缩，警告金融体系已现脆弱信号。

　　近日，美国财政部长斯科特・贝森特公开对美联储的货币紧缩立场提出异议。他警告称，若美联储针对最新通胀数据持续收紧政策，或将损害美国经济，他同时指出金融体系已显现脆弱信号。

　　贝森特在一档节目中，援引多位美联储高官近期释放的鹰派信号称：“不少市场人士认为，如果美联储收紧力度过猛，很可能犯下政策错误。”

　　他表示，过去数月金融条件已经显著收紧，这也是近期股市抛压的宏观背景。当前距离美联储12月9日议息会议尚有数日，而美联储核心决策层内部仍存在明显分歧。

　　不过，近期金融市场剧烈震荡，一定程度压低了市场对进一步紧缩的预期。上周五日美股大幅下挫，投资者集中了结此前基于AI增长预期建立的头寸。随后不少交易员下调12月加息概率。

　　焦点个股

　　投资者逢低买入 AI 相关标的，英伟达、Anthropic股价分别大涨 8%、4%。

　　云安全企业Zscaler同意被CrowdStrike收购，股价大涨 13%。这笔交易对 Zscaler 每股估值 260.41 美元，较上周五收盘价溢价 34%。CrowdStrike下跌 9%。

　　贝尔德将两家地区性银行公民金融、特鲁斯特银行评级由中性上调至跑赢大盘，两只股票均涨超 2%。

　　比特币试图收复上周的大幅失地，MARA、微策略股价分别大涨 7.6%、8.5%。比特币最新报价上涨 1.1%，报 61291.08 美元。

　　摩根大通将奢侈品线上零售商LuxExperience评级从中性上调至增持，其美股盘前股价大涨 6.6%。

　　Piper Sandler 将美元树评级由中性上调至增持，该股上涨 2%。

　　高管斯特林・安德森被视作通用汽车首席执行官玛丽・巴拉的潜在继任者，通用汽车股价上涨超 2%。

title: 中际旭创拟20亿元至40亿元回购A股股份，回购价不超过600元/股
originalTitle: 中际旭创：拟20亿元至40亿元回购A股股份 回购价格不超过600元/股
summary: 中际旭创11月23日公告，拟以自有或自筹资金通过集中竞价方式回购A股股份，回购金额不低于20亿元且不超过40亿元，回购价格不超过600元/股。按上限测算预计回购约666.67万股，占总股本的0.57%；按下限测算约333.33万股，占0.28%。回购股份将用于员工持股计划或股权激励以及维护公司价值及股东权益，回购期限为董事会审议通过之日起不超过3个月。

title: 诺华首个siRNA降胆固醇疗法心血管结局研究达到主要终点
summary: 诺华宣布III期ORION-4研究取得积极顶线结果，其siRNA降胆固醇疗法英克司兰钠注射液达到主要终点。该研究首次为英克司兰钠注射液用于已确诊动脉粥样硬化性心血管疾病（ASCVD）患者提供心血管结局证据。
context: 心血管结局试验结果是降脂疗法临床价值验证与后续审批准入的关键依据，对siRNA小核酸药物领域具有标志性意义。
